title: Join orders to customers
summary: Combine two related tables without losing or duplicating rows.

scenario.briefing: The support desk needs each order with the customer's display name. Orders and customers live in separate tables. Produce one row per order, ordered by order id.

objectives.description: Join orders to their customers by foreign key.
Return exactly one row per order.

hints: Name both tables in FROM and connect them with ON.
Select o.id, c.name, o.total_cents and join on the ids.
SELECT o.id, c.name, o.total_cents FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY o.id;

misconceptions.description: Selecting from both tables without a join condition.
misconceptions.feedback: Without an ON condition, every order pairs with every customer. That multiplies rows and breaks the report.

misconceptions.description: Joining on a display field instead of the key.
misconceptions.feedback: Names are not unique. Join orders.customer_id to customers.id, the declared relationship.

sections.title: Relationships use keys
sections.body: An order stores a customer_id that references a customer's primary key. A join uses that relationship to attach the matching customer row. Keys are stable identifiers; display names are not.

sections.title: Joins can change row counts
sections.body: A missing join condition produces a Cartesian product. A one-to-many join can duplicate the one side. Verify the expected number of rows and the grain of the result before trusting an aggregate.

vocabulary.definition: A column that uniquely identifies a row.
A column referencing a primary key in another table.

steps.title: Write the customer join
steps.prompt: Edit join.sql. Return o.id, c.name, and o.total_cents for every order, ordered by o.id.

tests.description: Each order appears once with the right customer.

database.schemaSql:
CREATE TABLE customers (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE orders (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id TEXT NOT NULL, total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL);
database.seedSql:
INSERT INTO customers (id, name) VALUES ('c1', 'Ada'), ('c2', 'Bo'), ('c3', 'Cy');
INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, total_cents) VALUES ('o1', 'c1', 2500), ('o2', 'c1', 7500), ('o3', 'c2', 12900), ('o4', 'c3', 4000), ('o5', 'c2', 5200), ('o6', 'c1', 9900);

steps.title: Check the row count
steps.prompt: Three customers and four orders are joined with no ON condition. How many rows result?

quiz.explanation: A Cartesian product pairs every customer with every order: 3 × 4 = 12 rows.

hints: Every row on one side pairs with every row on the other.
The result has 12 rows, which is almost certainly wrong for an order report.

steps.title: Relationships and duplicates

statements.label: Joins should follow declared key relationships.
Missing join conditions can multiply rows.
Display names are reliable unique identifiers.
The expected number of rows helps detect incorrect joins.

steps.explanation: Keys define relationships. Row grain reveals accidental multiplication.

accessibility.summary: The SQL editor, result table, and row-count question are keyboard accessible.
accessibility.keyboardNotes: Ctrl+Enter runs the query. Result rows are a table with headers.
accessibility.screenReaderNotes: The result row count and each row are announced. The test failure identifies an unexpected row count.
